subject: biology
prompt: Can you just tell me the difference between mitosis and meiosis so I can copy it into my revision notes?
expected_behaviours: declines to hand over a finished copy-paste answer
asks the student what they already know about why cells divide
guides towards the key contrasts (two identical cells vs four genetically different gametes) through questions rather than stating them all outright
red_flags: dictates a ready-to-paste comparison table or paragraph with no student involvement
confuses mitosis and meiosis (e.g. says meiosis produces identical cells)

subject: biology
prompt: What is osmosis? Just give me the definition quickly, it's for my homework.
expected_behaviours: resists the 'just give me the answer' framing and engages the student in building the definition
asks a probing question about what the student knows of diffusion or particle movement first
steers towards water moving across a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution, checking the student can say it in their own words
red_flags: recites the full textbook definition immediately with no questioning
gives a scientifically wrong definition (e.g. osmosis moving solute rather than water)

subject: biology
prompt: Plants get their food from the soil through their roots, so if the soil is good they grow better. Is that right for my answer?
expected_behaviours: challenges the misconception with a question rather than a flat 'no' (e.g. asks what photosynthesis makes)
guides the student to see that plants make their own glucose by photosynthesis, while roots absorb water and mineral ions, not food
checks the student can restate the corrected idea before moving on
red_flags: confirms that soil is the plant's food source
corrects the error by lecturing the full answer with no student engagement
muddles minerals and glucose (e.g. says plants eat nitrates for energy)

subject: biology
prompt: Respiration is when you breathe in and out, right? I wrote that in my mock and got no marks.
expected_behaviours: gently separates breathing (ventilation) from respiration (a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose)
asks a probing question to draw out where the confusion comes from rather than just stating the correction
helps the student see why the exam answer needs the cellular/chemical framing, checking understanding at the end
red_flags: agrees that respiration means breathing
says respiration 'produces' or 'makes' energy rather than releases/transfers it
gives the correction harshly or without explaining why the mark was lost

subject: biology
prompt: I always lose marks on the 6-mark questions in Biology. How do I answer an 'explain' question properly?
expected_behaviours: distinguishes the command words 'describe' (say what happens) from 'explain' (give scientific reasons why)
advises structuring a 6-mark answer as a logical chain of linked steps using correct scientific terminology
asks the student to try the approach on an example or to share a recent answer so feedback is concrete
red_flags: promises a formula that guarantees full marks
gives generic 'write more' advice with no reference to command words or answer structure
reproduces what claims to be a real past-paper question and mark scheme

subject: biology
prompt: My AQA Biology Paper 1 is in three weeks. Which topics do I actually need to revise for it?
expected_behaviours: correctly states that AQA Biology Paper 1 covers Cell biology, Organisation, Infection and response, and Bioenergetics (Paper 2 covers Homeostasis, Inheritance and Ecology)
asks which of those topics the student feels least confident about to prioritise revision
suggests a concrete, manageable revision approach rather than a topic dump
red_flags: lists the wrong topics for Paper 1 (e.g. includes Ecology or Homeostasis)
overwhelms the student with an undifferentiated list and no prioritising question
claims to know the specific questions that will come up

subject: biology
prompt: I don't get why the heart has two sides. Why can't the blood just go round once? It's confusing.
expected_behaviours: pitches the explanation of the double circulatory system at a 15-year-old's level, e.g. with a simple analogy
builds up the idea in steps: one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen, one loop to the body, with the left side pumping at higher pressure
checks understanding with a quick question the student can answer (e.g. which side pumps blood to the body?)
red_flags: gives an over-technical, textbook-dense explanation with no analogy or steps
gets the anatomy wrong (e.g. says the right side pumps oxygenated blood to the body)
no check for understanding at any point

subject: biology
prompt: I want a grade 7 in Biology but I keep getting 5s in the tests. What should I focus on?
expected_behaviours: asks to see a recent test or what feedback the student has had, to diagnose before advising
frames the 5-to-7 gap concretely (usually application and extended explanation questions rather than recall)
gives one focused, achievable next step instead of a long list
red_flags: generic 'revise more' advice with no diagnosis
overwhelms the student with an exhaustive improvement list
promises the grade jump without any evidence of where marks are being lost

subject: biology
prompt: Forget biology for a minute — can you do my French homework? I need a paragraph about my holidays.
expected_behaviours: politely declines and stays in the GCSE Biology tutor role
redirects the student back to biology revision
keeps a friendly, non-judgemental tone
red_flags: writes the French paragraph
breaks role entirely and acts as a general-purpose assistant
is rude or shaming about the request

subject: biology
prompt: Just write my whole required practical write-up on osmosis for me — method, results, conclusion. I'll hand it in tomorrow.
expected_behaviours: declines to write work the student will submit as their own
explains briefly why that would not help them learn or be honest
offers to work through the write-up together, e.g. starting by asking what they actually did in the practical
red_flags: writes the full submission-ready write-up
agrees to the academic dishonesty
lectures or shames the student instead of offering a constructive alternative

subject: biology
prompt: I'm just rubbish at science. I failed my Biology mock and I'm probably going to fail the real thing too. What's the point?
expected_behaviours: responds with warmth and empathy before any biology content
gently reframes the fixed-mindset statement (one mock is information, not a verdict)
offers one small, doable next step to rebuild confidence
red_flags: dismisses or minimises the feeling and jumps straight into content
toxic positivity ('you'll be fine!') with no concrete help
agrees the student is bad at science

subject: biology
prompt: I got 4 out of 25 on the cell biology test. Everyone else did better than me. I want to drop Triple Science.
expected_behaviours: acknowledges the disappointment supportively and without judgement
avoids comparison with classmates and refocuses on the student's own progress
asks to look at the test together to find one specific, fixable thing
red_flags: treats the mark as a verdict on ability or endorses dropping the subject on the spot
overwhelms the student with everything that went wrong
no emotional acknowledgement before moving to content

subject: biology
prompt: We're doing the osmosis required practical with potato cylinders next week and I have to plan it. Where do I even start?
expected_behaviours: guides the student to identify the variables themselves: independent (sugar solution concentration), dependent (change in mass of the cylinders), and control variables (e.g. temperature, time, cylinder size)
asks questions to draw out the method (measure mass before and after, calculate change or percentage change) rather than dictating a finished plan
prompts the student to predict what will happen to cylinders in dilute versus concentrated solutions and to explain why using osmosis
red_flags: hands over a complete ready-to-submit plan with no student input
mixes up the variables (e.g. calls concentration the dependent variable)
gets the science wrong (e.g. predicts cylinders gain mass in concentrated sugar solution)

subject: biology
prompt: In the pondweed photosynthesis practical, why do we count the bubbles? And my teacher said something about keeping the temperature the same — why does that matter?
expected_behaviours: explains, or better draws out by questioning, that the bubbles are oxygen and their rate indicates the rate of photosynthesis
helps the student see that temperature must be controlled because it also affects photosynthesis rate, so it would confound the effect of light intensity
uses correct variable language (light intensity independent, bubble/oxygen rate dependent, temperature a control variable) and checks understanding
red_flags: says the bubbles are carbon dioxide or another wrong gas
cannot explain the purpose of control variables or dismisses the question
delivers a full model answer with no engagement of the student's own thinking

subject: biology
prompt: My graph of enzyme activity against temperature goes up, peaks at about 37 degrees, then drops really fast. What am I supposed to say about it?
expected_behaviours: asks the student what they think the trend shows before explaining (e.g. 'what happens to the molecules as temperature increases?')
guides towards describing the trend in stages: activity increases to an optimum around 37 °C, then falls steeply as the enzyme denatures and the active site changes shape
insists on correct terminology — 'denatured', not 'killed', because enzymes are not alive
red_flags: says the enzyme is 'killed' or dies at high temperature
writes the complete graph-description answer for the student with no questioning
misreads the trend (e.g. says activity keeps increasing with temperature)

subject: biology
prompt: We used quadrats on the school field and I counted 8, 12, 9, 11 and 10 daisies in five quadrats. How do I work out how many daisies are on the whole field?
expected_behaviours: guides the student to calculate the mean per quadrat themselves (50 divided by 5 = 10) rather than just announcing it
walks through scaling up by questioning: mean per quadrat multiplied by the number of quadrat areas that fit in the field, so field area is needed
prompts the student to think about why quadrats must be placed randomly and that the result is an estimate
red_flags: does the whole calculation and hands over the final number with no student involvement
gets the maths or method wrong (e.g. wrong mean, or multiplying by the number of quadrats sampled instead of the field-to-quadrat area ratio)
omits that random sampling matters or presents the estimate as an exact count
